summary: Fourteen days of high-quality closed-loop AAPS/Nightscout data (98.7% CGM coverage) show overall time-in-range of 86.0% with average glucose 121.6 mg/dL, alongside recurring level-2 hypoglycemia clusters, two unexplained severe hyperglycemia clusters, and a repeating late-morning-to-afternoon rise followed by an evening-to-overnight low. No carbohydrate entries exist anywhere in the package and the user has not declared a meal-timing or bolus-percentage strategy, so the observed therapy is entirely SMB/UAM correction-driven with zero carb counting. The leading, but not fully proven, explanation links a long 10-hour DIA and dynamic-ISF-driven large corrections at high glucose to a prolonged insulin tail that plausibly produces the delayed lows; a competing/contributing explanation is that user-set 135 mg/dL temporary targets may suppress SMB correction during the same afternoon window. Loose max IOB and max basal ceilings relative to estimated total daily dose add limited protective margin against IOB stacking. No profile parameter change is supported by the current evidence; the priority is safety review and single-variable verification before any profile or automation change.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM coverage is strong (98.7%, 5-min cadence, 10 gaps, largest 65 min, no duplicates/invalid entries). Zero carbohydrate entries exist in telemetry and COB is 0 in every loop status, confirming a genuine no-carb-counting therapy pattern rather than an export gap. A Profile Switch event on 2026-08-13 correlates with the current flat-ISF profile description, but profile_context declares historical_applicability as yes for the full period, so the current aaps_profile is treated as authoritative for all 14 days per governance rule, with residual low-weight uncertainty only.

analysis_steps.findings: Aggregate time-below-range is 5.1%, above typical target, with recurrent level-2 hypoglycemia clusters on 2026-08-13, 2026-08-14, and 2026-08-21, and two severe hyperglycemia clusters exceeding 285 mg/dL on 2026-08-15 and 2026-08-18 that are not explained by the single logged occlusion event (which falls on 2026-08-19). Several days show simultaneous elevated time-above-range and time-below-range, suggesting oscillation rather than a single directional bias. Local-hour analysis shows TBR peaks at hours 0-2 and hour 18, immediately following the afternoon hyperglycemia peak (hours 13-17).

analysis_steps.findings: Hours 3-7 local, under the 0.6-0.8 U/h basal steps and 90 mg/dL target, show excellent control (TIR 95-99%). Hours 0-2 local show elevated TBR (11.4-18.5%) despite unremarkable averages, consistent with either the overnight basal level or a residual IOB tail from evening corrections; these two explanations are not yet separable. Hours 8-9 local show a sharp post-breakfast rise coinciding with the CR 13.2 g/U segment start, more consistent with an unlogged meal effect than a basal defect. Hour 16 local is the day's worst window (TIR 67.9%, TAR 32.1%) even though basal steps down to 0.5 U/h at that hour, arguing against a pure basal-deficiency explanation and favoring a delayed correction/IOB catch-up or temp-target-suppression dynamic. Hour 18 local shows the day's highest TBR (15.3%) immediately after the afternoon peak, consistent with an overcorrection tail rather than an intrinsic defect of the 18:00 basal step.

analysis_steps.findings: CR segments cannot be validated against any carbohydrate ground truth since none exists; the counterintuitive pairing of the strongest CR ratio (10.5 g/U at 16:00) with the day's worst hyperglycemia hour suggests the cause may be an earlier meal bleeding forward rather than the 16:00 CR value itself, but this is unconfirmed. The profile declares a single flat ISF of 56 mg/dL/U, while dynamic_sensitivity_enabled=true with a 70% adjustment factor produces effective variable_sens values ranging from 27.8 to 178.7 mg/dL/U across loop statuses, a greater than sixfold spread; this means apparent ISF mismatches may reflect dynamic-ISF algorithm behavior rather than a wrong static profile value. DIA is 10 hours, longer than typical for rapid-acting insulin; multiple therapy_response_windows show glucose changes still moving substantially at the 240-360 minute marks (for example -173 mg/dL at 360 min on 2026-08-14 and -176 mg/dL at 360 min on 2026-08-19), supporting a plausible but unconfirmed IOB-stacking mechanism linking large dynamic-ISF-driven corrections to the delayed hypoglycemia already identified in basal_targets.

analysis_steps.findings: COB is 0 in every loop status, confirming SMB/UAM-only, no-carb-counting operation, consistent with smb_always_enabled=true and uam_enabled=true. Several 135 mg/dL temporary targets fall inside or adjacent to the worst afternoon hyperglycemia window; combined with smb_with_temp_target_enabled=true and smb_with_high_temp_target_enabled=false, this raises a plausible but only partially evidenced hypothesis that SMB correction may be suppressed during some of these windows, since correction boluses were still logged on some but not all affected days. smb_interval_minutes, max_smb_basal_minutes, and max_uam_smb_basal_minutes show no evidence of driving observed highs or lows.

analysis_steps.findings: autosens_enabled=false with dynamic_sensitivity_enabled=true is an internally consistent configuration, not a conflict; sensitivity_ratio values near 1 are neutral adjustments and are correctly distinguished from the much wider variable_sens swings used for actual dosing. The lowest variable_sens values (most aggressive effective ISF) occur during high, fast-rising glucose and correspond to the largest computed insulin_req and temp basal rates (up to 4 U/h), which combined with the 10-hour DIA is the strongest available unifying hypothesis for the delayed evening/overnight hypoglycemia, though it remains correlational. max_iob_units (25 U) and max_basal_u_per_hour (12 U/h) are large relative to the profile's 0.5-0.8 U/h basal segments and the period's estimated average total daily dose of approximately 19.7 U/day, providing limited protective margin against IOB stacking; any tightening must not be evaluated together with a DIA or ISF change.

analysis_steps.findings: The most defensible unifying explanation across stages links a long 10-hour DIA with dynamic-ISF-driven large corrections at high glucose to a prolonged insulin tail, plausibly producing the recurring hour 0-2 and hour 18 local hypoglycemia; this competes with, and is not fully separable from, possible SMB suppression during 135 mg/dL temporary targets in the same afternoon window, and from the complete absence of carbohydrate logging which blocks any meal-effect confirmation. No profile segment shows evidence strong enough to support a concrete value change; the two unexplained severe hyperglycemia clusters and the loose max IOB/max basal ceilings are flagged as safety-relevant items for sequential, single-variable review rather than immediate change. Recommended order: review DIA/insulin-action assumptions first, then max IOB/max basal ceilings, then SMB high-temp-target behavior, then begin carbohydrate logging to resolve the meal-effect uncertainty.

implementation_steps: Discuss the recurring hypoglycemia clusters (2026-08-13, 2026-08-14, 2026-08-21) and the two unexplained severe hyperglycemia clusters (2026-08-15, 2026-08-18) with a diabetes care provider before making any setting change

education: Duration of insulin action (DIA) determines how long insulin-on-board is assumed to remain active; a longer DIA setting than the insulin's true action time can cause the algorithm to under-correct early and over-correct later, producing delayed hypoglycemia after large corrections

Dynamic ISF adjusts the effective sensitivity used for each dosing decision based on recent glucose behavior, while Autosens is a separate, currently disabled mechanism; a sensitivity_ratio near 1 reflects a neutral dynamic adjustment, not a disabled feature

Temporary targets can change how aggressively the algorithm doses corrections; whether a specific temporary target level is treated as a high temp target affects whether SMB dosing is suppressed during that period
Time-below-range and time-above-range occurring on the same day generally indicate oscillation between overcorrection and under-correction rather than a single consistent bias in one direction

Correction boluses respond to glucose that has already risen, while meal boluses are intended to act ahead of an anticipated rise; a therapy pattern with only correction boluses and no meal boluses is inherently reactive rather than anticipatory
safety_notes: This is decision-support content only; TuneMyBG prepares data for review and does not provide medical advice
The user must independently verify every proposed change with a qualified diabetes care provider before applying it
Any change should be made one at a time, with sufficient observation time before making the next change
Glucose should be monitored closely after any change, with particular attention to the previously identified overnight and evening hypoglycemia windows
Do not change dependent insulin-delivery settings such as DIA, ISF, and IOB/basal safety ceilings at the same time, since their combined effects cannot be separated from a single evaluation period

The two unexplained severe hyperglycemia clusters and the recurrent hypoglycemia clusters should be flagged to a care provider as a priority safety discussion before any routine profile optimization is pursued
